lessonRef.unitTitle: PF2 — Buying Goods and Services: Comparing a Purchase Before You Make It
lessonRef.title: Error and misconception analysis: price, quality, and fitness for purpose

focus: price, quality, and fitness for purpose
objective: Test the claim that a higher price means better quality against fictional rating data, find the counterexample that breaks it, and quantify what the extra money bought.
scenario: A fictional product reviewer wrote: "With blenders, you get what you pay for — the more it costs, the better it is." The four invented models and their made-up durability ratings below are the data the reviewer had.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional rating table in these directions

tasks.directions: The four fictional models, with price and durability rating out of 5: Model W $39, rated 3.8. Model X $72, rated 4.4. Model Y $118, rated 3.1. Model Z $155, rated 4.5.

prompts.text: Which pair of models directly contradicts the claim that a higher price means a better rating?

tasks.directions: Quantify the counterexample and put every model on one scale.

prompts.text: How much more does Model Y cost than Model X?
What does Model X cost per rating point? Round to the nearest cent.
What does Model Y cost per rating point?
What does Model W cost per rating point?
What does Model Z cost per rating point?
State precisely what is wrong with the reviewer’s claim, using the data, and write a version of the claim that the same four models would actually support.

remediation: If the counterexample is hard to spot, sort the four models by price and read the ratings down the column: 3.8, 4.4, 3.1, 4.5. A rule that price predicts rating would need that column to rise every time, and it falls once.
extension: Add a fictional Model V at $95 rated 4.8 and say whether it changes the reviewer’s claim, the cost-per-point ranking, or both.
